USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay in the G20 90-day window and press Beijing for enforceable structural commitments on IP, forced tech transfer, and industrial policy—do not raise List 3 to 25% now, and do not trade away tariff leverage for a purchases-only deal. Treat the just-concluded Beijing working-level talks as the start of a process, not a settlement: lock in any farm/energy purchase offers as a down payment, keep the March 2 hike as unused leverage, and keep the Meng extradition on a legal track rather than as a bargain chip. A new tariff or entity-list wave this week would likely blow up talks, deepen farm-belt losses, and feed the December growth scare already visible in U.S. markets and sentiment.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not high or existential. Combined Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B, and China has matched on the $50B lists plus 5–10% tariffs on ~$60B of U.S. goods, with soybeans, autos, and aircraft explicitly targeted (timeline 2018-06-15 through 2018-09-24). That retaliation is biting a politically important export sector: U.S. soybean sales to China for Jan–Oct 2018 were 63% below 2017, mid-October sales were down ~94% from the prior harvest, and New Orleans export prices fell from about $10.89 to $8.68/bu after the 25% Chinese soybean tariff. Consumer sentiment dropped from 98.3 in December to 91.2 in January, the VIX spiked to 36.07 on 2018-12-24 and was still ~20 on 2019-01-09, and the 10-year yield slid from a November peak near 3.24% to 2.74%—a growth-scare signature, not a recession print. Industrial production is only slightly softer and CPI is stable, so this is not yet a material GDP crisis. The Dec 1 Meng arrest and China’s detention of Kovrig and Spavor add alliance and tech-security risk that can poison talks, but they have not collapsed the channel: Beijing working-level talks ran Jan 7–9, were extended a day, and showed progress on purchases (another large soybean buy; five GM-crop approvals) while remaining far apart on structural reform and enforcement. That mix—usable U.S. leverage, concentrated farm pain, market/sentiment stress, and an open but incomplete negotiation—sits between the 0.0 and +0.5 USA anchors, hence +0.22. Action should stay near zero: the May 19 “trade war on hold” statement collapsed within ten days when the U.S. proceeded after a purchases-only joint statement, so conceding rollbacks or locking in purchases without verification would repeat that error. Escalating tariffs now would also be premature—the Jan 1 List 3 hike is already suspended as the bargaining chip, talks just ended constructively, and a further hike would hit more consumer goods and invite another retaliation cycle. Negotiate without new commitments until a verifiable structural package exists.
key_factors: 90-day G20 truce with unused March 2 List 3 hike (10%→25% on ~$200B) as leverage
Beijing Jan 7–9 talks: purchase/market-access progress, structural IP/tech-transfer and enforcement still open
China ag retaliation: soy exports to China down sharply, farm-belt price and inventory pressure
U.S. financial/sentiment stress (VIX spike, 10y yield drop, UMCSENT 91.2) without a clear industrial recession
Meng extradition plus Kovrig/Spavor detentions raise political risk if trade and legal tracks are fused
May 2018 purchases-only “truce” collapsed—do not settle for the same bargain

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended (tariffs remain at 10%). Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou...
Trade talks resume in Beijing (working / mid-level). China discusses increased purchases of US goods; structural issues remain open.
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
China detains Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor (widely viewed as retaliation for the Meng arrest; Beijing denies linkage).
University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment fell to 91.2 on 2019-01-01 from 98.3 in December (change -5.0, about -5.2%).
VIX closed 36.07 on 2018-12-24 and 19.98 on 2019-01-09, still well above mid-2018 teens.
10-year Treasury yield 2.74% on 2019-01-09 after an early-November peak of 3.24%.
Progress on U.S. farm and energy purchases and market access; sides further apart on structural reforms to stop alleged IP theft/forced tech transfer and on how to hold Beijing to its promises.

Soybean exports to China for January through October 2018 are 63% lower than the same period in 2017; China levied 25% retaliatory tariffs on U.S. soybeans, more than half of 2017 U.S. soybean exports.
If no deal is reached by March 2, Trump has said he will raise tariffs to 25% from 10% on $200 billion of Chinese imports.
